prompt: Before arguing about whether a model is fair to an age group, what does the lesson do first?

choices.text: Prints the model's decisions band by band
choices.why: Yes. Rates, credits, recall and precision per band.

choices.text: Retrains the model with balanced class weights
choices.why: Lesson 13's remedy, for a different problem.

choices.text: Removes age from the data
choices.why: That is the instinct the next section tests.

choices.text: Asks the legal team for a ruling on which bands to protect
choices.why: That conversation needs the tables first.

prompt: With age in the model, what share of the 18-24 band's leavers got a credit? Answer as a decimal, three places.
The 65+ band shows recall 0.185 and precision 0.714. Why should Ana not act on those numbers yet?

choices.text: The oldest band leaves less often than the others
choices.why: It leaves at 7.3%, almost the highest.

choices.text: They are about five people
choices.why: Yes. 369 subscribers, about 27 leavers, five reached.

choices.text: Precision and recall cannot be computed for a single band
choices.why: They were, row by row.

choices.text: The model never saw anybody over 65 in training
choices.why: The training months include them too.

prompt: Taking age out cost R$ 336 in net value. What did it change that matters more?

choices.text: The AUC fell below 0.7
choices.why: The net value barely moved; the model is about as good.

choices.text: The number of subscribers in each band of the test months
choices.why: The rows are the same in both tables.

choices.text: Who gets the credit
choices.why: Yes. The young lost credits and the old gained them.

choices.text: The cut, which had to be recomputed
choices.why: Both use the same break-even cut.

prompt: Why did removing age make the youngest subscribers worse off?
hint: They leave more for reasons only age shows.

choices.text: Young subscribers have fewer orders
choices.why: Nothing in the section says so.

choices.text: The model then saw them as older than they were
choices.why: It does not guess an age; it lost a signal.

choices.text: The cut was raised for them
choices.why: There is one cut for everybody.

choices.text: It stopped recognising some of that band's leavers
choices.why: Yes. Recall fell from 0.267 to 0.194.

prompt: Leaving the protected column out of the model is called fairness through ___.
hint: The model is not aware of it.

prompt: Which position does the lesson recommend as a default?

choices.text: Keep it out of the model and keep it for measuring
choices.why: Yes. Without the column no table of this lesson can be printed.

choices.text: Delete the column from the data
choices.why: Then nobody can check what the model does to a group.

choices.text: Replace it with a random column
choices.why: That measures nothing.

choices.text: Use it openly in every model
choices.why: Only when the decision benefits the group and the reason survives being said.

prompt: How does the lesson test whether the kept columns carry age?

choices.text: It drops each column and compares net value
choices.why: That measures value, not age.

choices.text: It predicts age from them
choices.why: Yes. An AUC of 0.872 for 65 or over.

choices.text: It checks each column's correlation with churn
choices.why: Churn is not the question here.

choices.text: It reads the SHAP value of age
choices.why: The model without age has no SHAP value for it.

prompt: From columns without age, with what AUC did the model pick out subscribers aged 65 or over? Three decimal places.
Match each band to the share of it that uses the app.
A manager proposes listing every proxy for age and removing them all. What is the problem?

choices.text: Only `app_user` is a proxy
choices.why: Boleto and the missing login carry age too.

choices.text: The law requires proxies to be kept
choices.why: No law says that.

choices.text: Removing every correlated column would remove the model
choices.why: Yes. The defence is measurement.

choices.text: Proxies cannot be found by any test
choices.why: `proxies.py` found them.

prompt: Match each definition of fairness to the column of `by_age.py` it compares.
hint: The table at the top of the section.

prompt: Why can equal precision and equal recall not both hold across the bands here?

choices.text: Precision is not defined when a band gets no credits
choices.why: Every band got some credits.

choices.text: The bands have different numbers of subscribers in them
choices.why: Size adds noise; the conflict comes from base rates.

choices.text: The model was not tuned enough to reach both
choices.why: No tuning gets round it; it is a theorem.

choices.text: The bands leave at different rates
choices.why: Yes. Only a perfect model escapes that.

prompt: A bank flags transactions for a fraud check, which delays them. Which definition matters most?

choices.text: Predictive parity
choices.why: Yes. Being flagged should mean the same thing for everyone.

choices.text: None, since fraud is not a protected characteristic
choices.why: The groups being flagged can still be.

choices.text: Demographic parity, because every group should be checked equally often
choices.why: That ignores whether the checks are deserved.

choices.text: Equal opportunity
choices.why: That fits a benefit meant for those who need it.

prompt: According to the lesson, who chooses the definition of fairness?

choices.text: The data scientist
choices.why: It is not a technical choice.

choices.text: Whoever is responsible for the decision
choices.why: Yes. The tables inform it; they do not make it.

choices.text: Nobody: one definition is always correct
choices.why: Each fits different decisions.

choices.text: The algorithm, by maximising AUC
choices.why: AUC knows nothing about groups.

prompt: Net value was R$ 21,672 with one cut and R$ 20,584 with the same share in every band. What did equal shares cost, in reais?
Under equal shares, what happened to the youngest band?

choices.text: It stayed as it was
choices.why: Its share of credits moved.

choices.text: Its recall rose to match the oldest band's
choices.why: Equal shares equalises credits, not recall.

choices.text: It lost credits, though it leaves most
choices.why: Yes. 3.9% down to 3.0%.

choices.text: It got the most credits of every band
choices.why: Every band got the same share, 3.0%.

prompt: Which are cautions the lesson raises about a separate cut per age band? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It requires retraining the model for every band
choices.why: `parity.py` reuses one model.

choices.text: It always costs more than R$ 10,000
choices.why: Here it cost R$ 1,088.

choices.text: A quantile on 369 subscribers moves every month
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: It treats people differently by a protected characteristic
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: The legal team says: "Just remove age, and the problem is gone." Which reply does the lesson give?

choices.text: Ask for a bigger test set
choices.why: That does not answer the point.

choices.text: Refuse, because age is the model's best column
choices.why: Removing it cost only R$ 336.

choices.text: Agree, since a model without age cannot treat ages differently
choices.why: It still did, through the proxies.

choices.text: Removing it changed who benefits and left age in the decision
choices.why: Yes. Keep it out of the model and in the audit.

prompt: Marketing says: "It's a discount, not a loan. Nobody is harmed." What is the reply?

choices.text: A benefit withheld from one group is the harm
choices.why: Yes. Small stakes do not remove the question.

choices.text: The credit should be turned into a loan so the law applies
choices.why: Nothing of the kind.

choices.text: Correct, so no audit is needed
choices.why: Unequal treatment still counts.

choices.text: Discounts are not covered by data protection law
choices.why: The LGPD covers processing personal data, whatever it decides.

prompt: An engineer says: "The model is maths. It can't be biased." What does the lesson answer?
hint: Who chose the data and the objective?

choices.text: Agree, so long as age is not a column
choices.why: Proxies carry it anyway.

choices.text: It is as fair as its data and objective, chosen by people
choices.why: Yes. The tables show which way it leans.

choices.text: Maths can be wrong
choices.why: The arithmetic is right; what it learns from is the point.

choices.text: Only neural networks are biased
choices.why: This was boosted trees.

prompt: A subscriber asks why they were not offered a credit. What does Ana's frame commit to?

choices.text: Publishing the whole model so anybody can read the weights
choices.why: A boosted model's weights explain nothing.

choices.text: Sending everybody who asks a credit
choices.why: That is a different policy, and an expensive one.

choices.text: An answer, made possible by the SHAP values
choices.why: Yes. Lesson 19's explanations make it answerable.

choices.text: Never answering, to protect the model
choices.why: The LGPD gives a right to ask for review.

prompt: Order the steps of Ana's monthly fairness audit.
items: Score the month's subscribers with the live model
Split them by the age kept for audit
Print each band's recall with a bootstrap interval
Investigate a band whose recall falls clearly below

prompt: A new model reads `postcode`. Before it goes live, what does this lesson say to do?

choices.text: Drop `postcode` at once, since postcodes are always proxies for something protected
choices.why: There is no list to remove; removing everything removes the model.

choices.text: Leave it as it is, if the protected columns are not in it
choices.why: Proxies carry them anyway.

choices.text: Give every postcode the same share of credits
choices.why: That is a policy with a price, decided later if at all.

choices.text: Print the tables by group, and test what `postcode` predicts
choices.why: Yes. The defence is measurement.
